description: Core Swahili building blocks for English speakers at A2, in Standard Swahili (Tanzania and Kenya).

terms.definition: Links a person or thing to what it is: am, is, are. It stays the same for every person.
terms.example: Jina langu ni Amina, mimi ni jirani yako. — My name is Amina, I'm your neighbour.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Mimi ni nyumbani' for 'I'm at home': where you are takes -ko, so 'Niko nyumbani'.

terms.definition: Marks an action happening now or done as a habit. It goes between the person prefix and the verb.
terms.example: Tunakunywa chai sasa. — We're having tea now.
terms.discussion: The person prefixes are ni- (I), u- (you), a- (he/she), tu- (we), m- (you all) and wa- (they).

terms.definition: Says what you want: a thing, or an action with ku- + verb after it.
terms.example: Nataka chai bila sukari, tafadhali. — I want tea without sugar, please.
terms.discussion: In speech ninataka shortens to nataka. You'll hear nataka far more, and it's fine in a shop.

terms.definition: Tells where someone is, or how they are right now. Add a person prefix: niko, uko, yuko.
terms.example: Uko wapi? Niko sokoni. — Where are you? I'm at the market.
terms.discussion: For he or she it's yuko, not ako. The negative swaps the prefix: siko, huko, hayuko.

terms.definition: Says something exists or is available: there is, there are. Hakuna means there isn't any.
terms.example: Kuna mkate leo? — Is there any bread today?
terms.discussion: Hakuna matata is real Swahili, but in daily life people mostly say hakuna shida: no problem.

terms.definition: Puts an action in the past. Use person prefix + -li- + verb: nilikula, I ate.
terms.example: Jana tulikwenda sokoni na mama. — Yesterday we went to the market with Mum.
terms.anti_example: Not 'sililala' for 'I didn't sleep': the negative past uses -ku-, so 'sikulala'.

terms.definition: Means have, literally 'be with'. Nina, una, ana: I have, you have, he or she has.
terms.example: Una chenji? Nina elfu kumi tu. — Got change? I only have ten thousand.
terms.anti_example: Not 'si nina' for 'I don't have': say 'sina', and 'huna', 'hana' for you and him or her.

terms.definition: Makes a present action negative: use a negative prefix, drop -na-, and end the verb in -i.
terms.example: Sipendi samaki, asante. — I don't like fish, thanks.
terms.discussion: The negative prefixes: si- (I), hu- (you), ha- (he/she), hatu- (we), ham- (you all), hawa- (they).

terms.definition: Expresses must or have to. The verb after it usually ends in -e: lazima niende, I must go.
terms.example: Samahani, lazima niondoke sasa. — Sorry, I have to leave now.

terms.definition: Points an action to the future. Use person prefix + -ta- + verb: nitarudi, I'll come back.
terms.example: Nitamaliza kazi hii kesho asubuhi. — I'll finish this work tomorrow morning.

terms.definition: Shows you are able to do something. The action follows as ku- + verb: naweza kusoma.
terms.example: Unaweza kunisaidia, tafadhali? — Can you help me, please?
terms.discussion: Unaweza…? is also the polite way to ask a stranger for a favour.

terms.definition: Marks something already done that is still true now. Many states use it: nimechoka, I'm tired.
terms.example: Tumefika nyumbani salama. — We got home safely.
terms.anti_example: Not 'ninachoka' for 'I'm tired': that means 'I'm getting tired'. Say 'nimechoka'.

relationships.description: Ni says what someone is; -ko says where they are or how they are right now.
Same slot after the person prefix; only the time marker changes.
Nilikula is I ate, back then; nimekula is I have eaten, so I am full now.
